#### Back pain registries

In the U.S., many spine-related registries are device- or procedure-focused and hence recruit patients primarily from specialists. Outside the U.S., several prospective spine registries/cohorts have been established to study various aspects of back pain and while somewhat broader in scope, most still have a specialist focus [48-50]. In contrast, Costa and colleagues established an inception cohort of 973 primary care patients with acute (less than two weeks) low back pain [51], demonstrating both the feasibility and value of such an approach. Identifying patients early in the course allowed measurement of baseline factors that predicted progression and chronicity.

The Back Complaints in the Elders (BACE) consortium is an international group of investigators who have independently established prospective cohorts in a primary care setting to investigate back pain among seniors [52]. Investigators from the Netherlands, Australia and Brazil are collaborating to identify prognostic indicators leading to the transition from acute to chronic back pain in the elderly. The objectives of BOLD parallel those of BACE and similar study structures facilitate international comparisons.

#### Strengths of registries

A great advantage of registries is that patient enrollment is easier than intervention trials, so large sample sizes are feasible. This increases generalizability and the ability to detect rare events, such as complications.

#### Limitations of registries

Roovers highlighted the limitations of registries, including lack of proper control groups, confounding, bias, poor data quality control, and potential conflicts of interest due to industry sponsorship [53]. Due to these limitations, registries will never replace randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The most important limitation of registries in general is the lack of a pre-defined control group. However, we can identify important subgroups contained within the registry to use for comparative effectiveness evaluations, such as patients with and without early imaging, and use propensity-matched controls to minimize selection bias associated with treatment or diagnostic testing.

#### Analytic approach

In many registries, there may be a relatively small subgroup of interest (e.g., a treatment or diagnostic testing prevalence of 1 or 2%) and a large number of controls available for a comparative analysis of outcomes. As a general analytic approach in BOLD, we will evaluate cases in comparative studies using 3:1 matched controls with the nearest propensity score [31].

Propensity-based matching is a strategy for assembling similar groups of patients in the absence of randomization. We will use this method to select control patients who are

similar to patients who have selectively received the intervention of interest (e.g. early imaging). If we do not appropriately match controls on important baseline characteristics to patients who receive the intervention, there is a risk of obtaining biased results when comparing cases with controls due to confounding [31-37]. Propensity score matching aims to provide a valid estimate of the intervention effect by comparing patients who have and have not had the intervention and who also have similar observed characteristics.

For a given research question and set of patients, we will use logistic regression models (or multi-level logistic regression models for ordinal or multilevel treatments; e.g., levels of treatment dose) to generate a propensity score for each person, using variables that are significant predictors of the intervention of interest. We will then match the propensity score of each case who received the intervention to the nearest propensity scores (up to 3) available among control patients whose propensity scores lie within a caliper window of 0.2σ of the case index, where σ is a measure of variation in the propensity score distributions of cases and controls as given in Rosenbaum and Rubin [35]. If no control propensity scores fall within the caliper window of a particular index case, then the index case will be excluded from any analyses.

# Strengths and Limitations

The strengths of our study include the use of MR analysis to complement a conventional observational approach, which allowed us to better overcome bias arising from confounding, measurement error, and reverse causation. The use of a "triangulation approach" also allowed for greater confidence in causal inference when there was consistency between the different approaches.49 We were also able to limit bias arising from self-reporting and misclassification by using strict case definitions for both our observational and MR data sources. Although more relaxed case definitions may have improved the generalizability of results, potential bias arising from their use can be particularly problematic when using binary exposures in MR.50 An additional strength of our study was the use of 2-step MR for a mediation analysis. This allowed us to specifically quantify the proportion of our exposure's effect attributable to our proposed mediators. Finally, we extended our analysis to illustrate how our methodology could explore multiple mediators in the proposed pathway.

In our study, the use of MR demonstrated a discrepancy when observing the effects of mental health on CVD. When adjusting for confounding in our mediation analysis, we likely overadjusted in order to confidently isolate the effects of the mediator. The Back Complaints in the Elders (BACE) consortium is an international group of investigators who have independently established prospective cohorts in a primary care setting to investigate back pain among seniors [52]. #### Strengths of registries

A great advantage of registries is that patient enrollment is easier than intervention trials, so large sample sizes are feasible. This increases generalizability and the ability to detect rare events, such as complications.

Due to these limitations, registries will never replace randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The most important limitation of registries in general is the lack of a pre-defined control group. However, we can identify important subgroups contained within the registry to use for comparative effectiveness evaluations, such as patients with and without early imaging, and use propensity-matched controls to minimize selection bias associated with treatment or diagnostic testing.

If we do not appropriately match controls on important baseline characteristics to patients who receive the intervention, there is a risk of obtaining biased results when comparing cases with controls due to confounding [31-37]. For a given research question and set of patients, we will use logistic regression models (or multi-level logistic regression models for ordinal or multilevel treatments; e.g., levels of treatment dose) to generate a propensity score for each person, using variables that are significant predictors of the intervention of interest. ### Summary
This report examines the community of individuals experiencing chronic lower back pain (CLBP). The key entities within this community are pain catastrophising, pain intensity, and disability. Pain intensity significantly affects disability.: Pain intensity is a component of chronic pain and is a significant factor in the development and maintenance of disability in individuals with CLBP. The analysis reveals that depression and anxiety are associated, comorbid, and often co-occur in the same individuals. The text also suggests a causal relationship between depression and anxiety, as well as an increased risk of depression in individuals with anxiety. Additionally, the study of depression includes data from the UK Biobank, a large-scale health study, and the selected genetic variants for depression were obtained from the largest GWAS meta-analysis of 807,553 European-descent individuals. Furthermore, depression is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CAD), particularly in patients with diabetes. ### Key Findings Depression and anxiety are related mental health conditions: The text provides multiple instances of the association between depression and anxiety, suggesting that they are closely related emotional states. This relationship is further supported by the fact that they share similar symptoms and risk factors. Depression and anxiety are comorbid conditions: The text indicates that depression and anxiety often co-occur in the same individuals. This comorbidity is significant, as it can lead to more severe symptoms and increased healthcare costs. Depression is associated with an increased risk of CAD: The text suggests a causal relationship between depression and an increased risk of CAD, particularly in patients with diabetes. This association is supported by multiple pieces of evidence, including genetic studies and inverse-variance weighted (IVW) analysis. Depression is associated with insomnia: The text indicates that insomnia is associated with an increased risk of depression. This association is supported by multiple pieces of evidence, including genetic studies and the fact that insomnia symptoms/disorder are reported to independently increase the risk of subsequent depression in older persons. Depression is associated with multimorbidity: The text suggests that depression is associated with an increased risk of multimorbidity, a condition where an individual has two or more chronic diseases. This association is supported by multiple pieces of evidence, including the fact that depression increases the risk for onset of multimorbidity by 80–90%. ### Impact Rating: 8.5 The high impact severity rating is due to the prevalence of depression and anxiety, their comorbidity, and the associated health risks, including cardiovascular disease. ### Chronic Lower Back Pain Community: Pain Catastrophising, Pain Intensity, and Disability ### Summary This report examines the community of individuals experiencing chronic lower back pain (CLBP). The key entities within this community are pain catastrophising, pain intensity, and disability. The relationships between these entities reveal that pain catastrophising significantly influences pain intensity, which in turn affects disability. Alcohol consumption, stress, and sleep quality are also associated with pain intensity and disability. ### Key Findings Pain catastrophising is a significant factor in the experience of pain intensity.: Pain catastrophising, the tendency to magnify the threat value of pain, feel helpless in the presence of pain, and have a relative inability to prevent or inhibit pain-related thoughts, is a key entity within the chronic lower back pain community. Studies have shown that pain catastrophising is associated with increased pain intensity, negatively correlated with pain intensity, and influences the pain intensity experienced by participants. It can also influence the level of pain intensity and may mediate the effect of treatments like Pilates exercise and tai chi on pain intensity. Pain intensity significantly affects disability.: Pain intensity is a component of chronic pain and is a significant factor in the development and maintenance of disability in individuals with CLBP. Higher pain intensity is associated with higher disability, making it difficult for individuals to perform daily activities. Pain intensity may also influence disability by making it difficult for individuals to perform physical tasks and thus affect their ability to manage their disability. Alcohol consumption is associated with increased pain intensity and disability.: Alcohol consumption is associated with pain intensity and disability. Alcohol can exacerbate pain, contribute to disability, and lead to physical impairments. The amount of alcohol consumed by an individual, typically measured in standard drinks per week, is correlated with disability, and excessive drinking can lead to a worsening of both pain intensity and disability. Stress and perceived stress can increase pain intensity.: Stress and perceived stress can increase the perception of pain intensity in chronic lower back pain. Stress can exacerbate pain and vice versa, making it a significant factor in the experience of pain intensity. Perceived stress, the subjective experience of the appraisal and reaction to stressors, including their emotional and physical impact, can also affect physical state and exacerbate pain intensity. Sleep quality is associated with pain intensity.: Sleep quality is associated with pain intensity. People who report poorer sleep quality also report worse pain intensity, although the underlying cause is still unclear. Self-reported sleep quality and proportion of time in slow-wave sleep (SWS) are associated with next-day pain intensity. ### Impact Rating: 8.5 The high impact severity rating of 8.5 indicates that the entities within this community have a significant impact on the quality of life and functioning of individuals with chronic lower back pain. ### Community of Individuals Seeking Mental Health Care and Experiencing Chronic Lower Back Pain ### Summary This report focuses on a community of individuals who seek care from general practitioners for their mental health disorders and also experience chronic lower back pain. The community's entities are interconnected, with pain being a common factor that influences various aspects of their lives, including their health, economic resources, and daily activities. The entities are also associated with other factors such as fear avoidance beliefs, hardship, and unhealthy health behaviors. ### Key Findings The presence of chronic lower back pain is a common experience among the community members.: The text indicates that individuals in the community seek care from general practitioners for their mental health disorders and also experience chronic lower back pain. This pain is described as an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage. Hardship is associated with the community, particularly in relation to Medicare Insurance Coverage.: The presence of hardship, a state of severe and prolonged difficulty or distress, is associated with the community. This hardship may be caused by factors such as poverty or other adverse circumstances. The text suggests that those with financial difficulties may be more likely to rely on Medicare for health insurance. Fear avoidance beliefs are related to the community and may be important targets for early interventions.: Fear avoidance beliefs, as measured by a questionnaire, are associated with the community. These beliefs might be useful for early interventions, as they could be good screening variables for identifying individuals at risk for chronic pain. The text also suggests that fear avoidance beliefs might be important targets for early interventions to prevent further progression or complications. Unhealthy health behaviors, such as smoking and alcohol consumption, may be related to the community and contribute to the development or exacerbation of pain.: The text indicates that unhealthy health behaviors, such as smoking and alcohol consumption, are associated with the community. These behaviors may be related to pain, as they can contribute to its development or exacerbation. The International Association for the Study of Pain is related to the study of pain and the community.: The International Association for the Study of Pain is a professional organization dedicated to the study of pain and its mechanisms. The text indicates that this organization is related to the study of pain and the community, suggesting a connection between the community and the broader field of pain research. ### Impact Rating: 7.5 The community's impact severity rating of 7.5 indicates a significant influence on the individuals' health, well-being, and daily functioning due to chronic lower back pain and associated factors. ### Chronic Lower Back Pain Research Community: Fear Avoidance Beliefs Questionnaire (FABQ) and Associated Studies ### Summary This report presents an analysis of a community of researchers and studies centered around the Fear Avoidance Beliefs Questionnaire (FABQ), a tool used to assess fear avoidance beliefs about physical activity and work in patients with chronic lower back pain. The community includes various studies that investigate the relationship between FABQ and other measures such as Visual Analog Scale (VAS), Fear of Pain Questionnaire (FPQ), and Pictorial Fear of Activity Scale – Cervical (PFActS-C). The community also includes researchers such as McCracken, who have authored or co-authored multiple studies using FABQ and other questionnaires. ### Key Findings FABQ is a widely used tool in the community: The FABQ is a key tool in the community, with multiple studies using it to investigate fear avoidance beliefs in patients with chronic lower back pain. The tool is part of a questionnaire and consists of two subscales: FABQ-Physical Activity and FABQ-Work. McCracken is a prominent researcher in the community: McCracken is an author of multiple studies related to chronic pain and chronic lower back pain. They have used FABQ, FPQ, and other questionnaires in their research. McCracken has collaborated with other researchers such as Smyth, Gutiérrez-Martínez, and Zhao-O'Brien on various studies. FABQ is used in conjunction with other questionnaires: In addition to FABQ, other questionnaires such as FPQ, PFActS-C, Back Pain Scores, West Haven-Yale Multidimensional Pain Inventory (MPI), and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index are used in the community. These questionnaires are used to measure various aspects of pain, such as intensity, fear of activity, and the impact of pain on a person's life. FABQ is used in various studies: FABQ is used in a variety of studies, including those conducted by Guclu, Ramirez-Maestre, Kaka, Pruneti, Monticone, Ciccone, and George. These studies investigate the relationship between FABQ and VAS, as well as the relationship between FABQ and other measures such as fear of pain. The index primary care visit triggers the administration of the baseline questionnaire: The index primary care visit is significant in the community as it triggers the administration of the baseline questionnaire, which includes FABQ and other questionnaires. This allows for the collection of baseline data on fear avoidance beliefs and other aspects of pain. ### Impact Rating: 7.5 The impact severity rating of 7.5 indicates a significant contribution to the understanding and management of chronic lower back pain through the use of the FABQ and associated questionnaires. ### Chronic Lower Back Pain Community: Fear Avoidance Model and Associated Factors ### Summary This report provides an overview of the community centered around the Fear Avoidance Model (FAM) and its relationship with chronic lower back pain. The FAM is a psychological model that explains the development and maintenance of pain-related fear and avoidance behavior in individuals with chronic pain. The community includes various entities such as Fear of Pain (FOP), Patient Income (Pi), Random Effects Model, Correlation Coefficient, and Fibromyalgia Associated Musculoskeletal Pain, among others. The entities are interconnected through relationships such as influence, measurement, and association. ### Key Findings The Fear Avoidance Model (FAM) is a central component in understanding chronic lower back pain.: The FAM is a psychological model that explains the development and maintenance of pain-related fear and avoidance behavior in individuals with chronic pain. It is a key concept in several studies that have proposed direct and positive relationships between Fear of Pain (FOP) and Pain Intensity (Pi). Fear of Pain (FOP) is a significant factor in the Fear Avoidance Model.: FOP is a questionnaire that can be used to compute an effect size. It is influenced by the anticipated pain experience, which may vary with treatment status and pain location. FOP is also related to pain intensity and is often studied in the context of the FAM. Patient Income (Pi) is associated with Pain Intensity (Pi) in the Fear Avoidance Model.: Pi is a measure of financial situation. In the studies, Pi and Pi are associated as variables. The effect size in the meta-analysis is calculated based on the relationship between Fear Avoidance Beliefs and Pain Intensity. The effect size is also calculated from correlation coefficients for Pain Interference. Random Effects Model is used to compute the effect size estimate for the FOP–PI relation.: Random Effects Model is a statistical model that assumes that the effect size varies across studies due to differences in populations and methods. It is an analytic strategy used to compute an effect size estimate for the FOP–PI relation. Fibromyalgia Associated Musculoskeletal Pain is related to various pain locations in the Fear Avoidance Model.: Fibromyalgia Associated Musculoskeletal Pain is also examined for orofacial pain, lower extremity pain, shoulder and arm pain, hand fractures, lower leg, head, neck, arm, upper leg, chest/abdomen, and trigger finger. These pain locations are parts of the body where pain may occur and are potentially affected by the chronic lower back pain. ### Impact Rating: 8.5 The high impact severity rating is due to the significant role of the Fear Avoidance Model in understanding and managing chronic lower back pain, as well as its wide application in various pain locations and patient populations. ## Relationships: (Social Causation Theory: A theory that suggests that stressful financial circumstances might lead to the occurrence of new depressive symptoms or maintain previous depression. In essence, this is part of the same question that underlies efforts to reconsider psychiatric diagnoses using Research Domain Criteria (Young et al., 2017) to better recognise their heterogeneity in both aetiology and presentation.
